pages.title: LiteSpec Documentation
pages.intent: LiteSpec is a standard for building one business application from written rules that tools check, and this index lists every page of that standard in four groups. Developers and agents open it at the start of a task to find the page that states the rules for that task. A project applies only the folders named by its selection in `.litespec/project.yaml` (its size, shape, technology stacks, and extensions), so most readers need only a few groups.

pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: The Analyzers section explains the LiteSpec.Analyzers package, which checks .NET server code against the LiteSpec standard while the compiler runs and reports each break as an error in the editor and the build. The package checks layer boundaries, modeling in Domain, the layer that holds the business rules, naming across the shared kernel and modules projects, and traceability from code to records in every layer, with one assertion rule in test projects. It reports one error per rule, with a link from each error to the standard it enforces; the [Analyzer rules overview](rules/README.md) lists every rule. A backend developer uses these pages to install the package once and to clear each finding by fixing the code it names.

pages.title: Check .NET Code with the Analyzers
pages.intent: The LiteSpec Roslyn analyzers report breaks in LiteSpec .NET rules as compiler errors on every build, so a team sees each break in the editor instead of finding it in review. This guide installs the analyzer package once for the backend projects and their tests, shows how to read and fix the first errors, and records an exception for a deliberate departure. Each step names the standard it satisfies, and the guide adds no rule of its own.

pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: This index lists the 45 analyzer rules, one reference page per rule, grouped by the layers each rule runs in. A developer who meets an error opens the page with the same ID to see what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to fix the code. Each entry carries a 1-line summary of what the rule reports.

pages.title: LS1001: Domain References an Outer-Layer Concern
pages.intent: LS1001 is a compiler check that reports code in Domain, the layer that holds business rules, naming a persistence, web, messaging, or logging type, which would tie those rules to infrastructure they cannot test on their own. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to move the flagged use out of Domain.

pages.title: LS1002: Domain Declares an Enum
pages.intent: LS1002 is a compiler check that reports an enum declared in Domain, the layer that holds business rules, because an enum carries no behavior and no stable code for callers outside Domain. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to replace the enum with an abstract record and sealed cases.

pages.title: LS1003: Aggregate Has No State Record
pages.intent: LS1003 is a compiler check that reports an aggregate with no State record, where an aggregate is the type that owns a unit of business state that changes in one step. Loose lifecycle flags let callers combine states the business never allows. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to give the aggregate a State record.

pages.title: LS1004: State Case Is Not Sealed
pages.intent: LS1004 is a compiler check that reports a lifecycle state case in Domain, the layer that holds business rules, left open for extension, which lets a later type add states the business never defined. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to seal the case.

pages.title: LS1005: Domain Throws a Non-Domain Exception
pages.intent: LS1005 is a compiler check that reports a throw in Domain, the layer that holds business rules, of an exception that is not a DomainException subclass, which would reach the caller with no stable failure code and no business meaning. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to throw a DomainException subclass instead.

pages.title: LS1006: Domain Exception Is Misnamed or Open
pages.intent: LS1006 is a compiler check that reports a DomainException subclass in Domain, the layer that holds business rules, that is not sealed or whose name does not end in Exception, which hides which business rule failed. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to name and seal the exception.

pages.title: LS1007: Domain Event Is Not an Immutable Record
pages.intent: LS1007 is a compiler check that reports a domain event, a record of a completed business fact, that is not an immutable record, which would let callers change the fact after it was raised. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to make the event an immutable record.

pages.title: LS1008: Domain Uses Binary Floating Point
pages.intent: LS1008 is a compiler check that reports a double or float type in Domain, the layer that holds business rules, because binary rounding makes totals and equality checks on money and exact quantities quietly wrong. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to hold the value in decimal or a value object.

pages.title: LS1009: Domain Reads a Nondeterministic Value
pages.intent: LS1009 is a compiler check that reports a read of the clock, randomness, or a new identifier in Domain, the layer that holds business rules, because such reads answer differently on each call and tests cannot repeat them. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to pass the value in as an argument.

pages.title: LS1010: Repository Exposes a Query Surface
pages.intent: LS1010 is a compiler check that reports a repository interface in Domain, the layer that holds business rules, that exposes a query surface such as `IQueryable` or a database session. A repository loads and stores one aggregate, and a query surface would let any caller compose its own queries around the rules the aggregate protects. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to return aggregates and Domain types only.

pages.title: LS1011: Public Domain Contract Is Undocumented
pages.intent: LS1011 is a compiler check that reports a public type or member in Domain, the layer that holds business rules, without XML documentation, which leaves readers guessing which business constraint, result, or failure it represents. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to document the contract.

pages.title: LS1012: Identifier Is Not a Strongly Typed Value
pages.intent: LS1012 is a compiler check that reports an identifier in Domain, the layer that holds business rules, that is not a strongly typed value, because a raw Guid lets one record's identity flow into another record's slot with no compiler complaint. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to wrap the value in a strongly typed identifier.

pages.title: LS1013: Switch Leaves a Sealed Case to Its Discard Arm
pages.intent: LS1013 is a compiler check that reports a switch in Domain, the layer that holds business rules, over a state or closed-set record hierarchy that leaves a sealed case to its discard arm, because the C# compiler does not check the switch and the missed case reaches the discard arm at run time. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to give every sealed case its own arm.

pages.title: LS2001: Implementation Type Is Not Internal Sealed
pages.intent: LS2001 is a compiler check that reports a handler, validator, endpoint, or other implementation type in the Application, Infrastructure, WebApi, and Worker layers that is not internal and sealed, which would invite callers to depend on it directly instead of going through its interface. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to close the type.

pages.title: LS2003: WebApi Uses an MVC Controller
pages.intent: LS2003 is a compiler check that reports an MVC controller class in the WebApi project. A controller groups several HTTP operations behind shared filters and routing, while the .NET stack gives each operation its own endpoint class, so each route can be read and reviewed on its own. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to replace the controller with endpoints.

pages.title: LS2004: Command Handler Writes Through a Document Session
pages.intent: LS2004 is a compiler check that reports a command handler, the type that runs the state change, writing through a document session or database context instead of a repository, which bypasses the boundary that guards the aggregate. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to reach stored data through a Domain repository.

pages.title: LS2005: Handler Name Lacks Its Command or Query Suffix
pages.intent: LS2005 is a compiler check that reports a command or query handler, the type that runs a use case, whose name does not state which of the two it runs, so the model builder cannot tell a write from a read by its file name. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to complete the handler name.

pages.title: LS2006: Endpoint Name Lacks Its Suffix
pages.intent: LS2006 is a compiler check that reports an endpoint, the type that maps one use case to HTTP, whose name does not end in `Endpoint`, so the model builder cannot find it by its file name. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to complete the endpoint name.

pages.title: LS2007: Reaction or Job Name Hides Its Kind
pages.intent: LS2007 is a compiler check that reports a reaction or job, the type that answers a domain event or runs scheduled work, whose name does not say which trigger it answers, so the model builder cannot discover it by name. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to name the reaction or job for its trigger.

pages.title: LS2009: Result Part Not Named After Its Result
pages.intent: LS2009 is a compiler check that reports a result part, a type declared beside a use-case result and reached through its properties, whose name does not start with the result name, so a reader cannot tell which result the part belongs to. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to name the part after its result.

pages.title: LS2010: Repository Variable Not Named After Its Interface
pages.intent: LS2010 is a compiler check that reports a repository parameter, field, or local whose name does not follow its interface, so a reader cannot tell which aggregate the variable stages. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to name the variable after its interface.

pages.title: LS2011: Query Handler Takes a Repository
pages.intent: LS2011 is a compiler check that reports a query handler, the type that answers a read, taking a Domain repository in its constructor, which pulls an aggregate into a read that should project past it. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to reach read data through the read session.

pages.title: LS2012: Handler Authorizes Itself
pages.intent: LS2012 is a compiler check that reports a command or query handler, the type that runs a use case, authorizing itself instead of leaving authorization to the pipeline guard. A handler authorizes itself when it throws an access refusal or when it takes the authorization guard. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to move the check into the declared access.

pages.title: LS2013: Audit Value Read from the Message in the Handler
pages.intent: LS2013 is a compiler check that reports a command handler, the type that runs the state change, adding an audit value that the message already carries, which the pipeline should have recorded before the handler ran. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to declare the value beside the message.

pages.title: LS2014: Command Handler Finds or Creates
pages.intent: LS2014 is a compiler check that reports a command handler, the type that runs the state change, that both finds a record and creates it in one method, hiding two use cases behind one name. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to split the flow across the boundary that owns it.

pages.title: LS2015: Command Handler Changes Records in a Loop
pages.intent: LS2015 is a compiler check that reports a command handler, the type that runs the state change, changing records in a loop, where one failing record rolls back the batch and the batch holds locks for its whole length. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to move the work into a job.

pages.title: LS2016: Handler Takes a Pipeline-Owned Collaborator
pages.intent: LS2016 is a compiler check that reports a command or query handler, the type that runs a use case, taking a collaborator the pipeline owns, such as the unit of work or the outbox, which no handler should touch directly. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to leave the collaborator to its owner.

pages.title: LS2017: LiteSpecLayer Names No Known Layer
pages.intent: LS2017 is a compiler check that reports a `LiteSpecLayer` project value naming no known layer under the `layer-projects` extension, so a misspelled value cannot silently turn the analyzers off. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to name the layer.

pages.title: LS2018: File Names a Type Outside Its Layer
pages.intent: LS2018 is a compiler check that reports an Application or WebApi file naming a type outside its layer, because a reference against the layer direction couples the file to work its layer never owns. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to name only the types the layer allows.

pages.title: LS2019: Use Case Names a Type of Another Use Case
pages.intent: LS2019 is a compiler check that reports a use case folder naming a type declared in another use case folder, because a reference between two slices couples work that changes for different reasons. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to move the shared type to the folder that owns it.

pages.title: LS2020: Module Names a Type Outside Another Module's Contracts
pages.intent: LS2020 is a compiler check that reports a module naming another module's type outside its `Contracts/` folder, because a read past the public surface couples the caller to internals the owner may change. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to read through the contracts the owner publishes.

pages.title: LS3001: Asynchronous Method Name Lacks Async
pages.intent: LS3001 is a compiler check that reports an async method whose name does not end in Async, which reads as a plain call where it is used, so readers miss the await and the cancellation token it needs. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to complete the name.

pages.title: LS3004: Concrete Class Is Not Sealed
pages.intent: LS3004 is a compiler check that reports a concrete class with no derived type that is not sealed, which reads as designed for extension, so readers subclass it where the author meant no one to extend it. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to seal the class or show it is built for extension.

pages.title: LS4001: Test Contains No Assertion
pages.intent: LS4001 is a compiler check that reports a test method that contains no assertion, because a test that asserts nothing passes whatever the code does and proves nothing about the scenario it names. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to assert the result the test covers.

pages.title: LS5001: Code Element Carries No Mark
pages.intent: LS5001 is a compiler check that reports a code element of a recognized kind that carries no mark naming the record it serves, because without the mark no tool can tell which record the element implements. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to add the missing mark.

pages.title: LS5002: Mark Names No Usable Record
pages.intent: LS5002 is a compiler check that reports a mark naming no record, a record of a type its code element does not take, or a mark on a type or method that takes no mark, because a mark pointing nowhere leaves the element unlinked. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to name a record the element takes.

pages.title: LS5003: Code Element Carries the Wrong Number of Marks
pages.intent: LS5003 is a compiler check that reports a code element carrying more or fewer marks than its kind takes, because an extra mark answers the element to a record it does not serve. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to carry exactly the marks the kind takes.

pages.title: LS5004: Mark Uses the Undeclared Style
pages.intent: LS5004 is a compiler check that reports a mark written in the style the project did not declare, because two styles in one project send each search to half the code. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to write the mark in the declared style.

pages.title: LS5005: Runtime Value Differs from Its Record
pages.intent: LS5005 is a compiler check that reports a hand-written event `Classification` or exception `Code` differing from what its record states, because a second copy of a record value drifts from the record. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to let the record decide the value.

pages.title: LS5006: Marked Event or Exception Is Not Partial
pages.intent: LS5006 is a compiler check that reports a marked domain event or rule exception not declared as a `partial` type, because the generator cannot add the runtime value to a type with no second part. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to declare the type partial.

pages.title: LS5007: Marked Act Raises an Undeclared Event
pages.intent: LS5007 is a compiler check that reports an aggregate method marked with a use case raising an event the use case does not list in `raises`, because an unlisted event starts a consequence nobody reviewed. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to declare or drop the event.

pages.title: LS5008: Declared Event Is Raised by No Marked Act
pages.intent: LS5008 is a compiler check that reports a use case listing an event in `raises` that no method marked with it raises, because a listed event no method raises is a promise the code does not keep. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to raise or unlist the event.

pages.title: LS5009: Two Permissions Generate One Constant Name
pages.intent: LS5009 is a compiler check that reports two permission records whose names generate the same constant, because the generator writes one constant per permission and cannot name two records with one name. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to rename one of the permissions.

pages.title: LS5011: One Message Maps to Two Use Cases
pages.intent: LS5011 is a compiler check that reports a message two marked handlers serve with different use cases, because the registry answers each message's use case and grant from one entry. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to give the message one use case.

pages.title: LS5012: Role Allows an Undeclared Permission
pages.intent: LS5012 is a compiler check that reports a role record allowing a permission no permission record declares, because the generator writes each role's allowed permissions from the shared permission list. This page states what the rule reports, where the error sits, and how to declare the permission or remove it from the role.

pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: The backend pages state how a LiteSpec server application is built: its layers, business model, coordination of use cases, storage, HTTP boundary, testing, and record identifiers, with the stack binding that realizes each one. A use case is one command or query with its access, results, and scenarios; a reaction answers an event without a request, and a job runs work on a schedule or by hand. A server project applies these pages through its stack, while a product without a server applies only the architecture, domain, application, and identifier pages, so every reader finds the rules for the layers their product has and no others.

pages.title: HTTP API
pages.intent: The WebApi layer is the thin HTTP boundary of a LiteSpec backend: it converts each HTTP request into a message for the Application layer, dispatches it, and maps the result back to a stable HTTP response. This page states what one endpoint owns, how routes, errors, and collection paging behave, and how the OpenAPI contract, the machine-readable description of the API, is generated from the code. Keeping business rules, storage, and provider calls out of endpoints keeps HTTP replaceable transport, so the API evolves without touching business behavior.

pages.title: Application Layer
pages.intent: The Application layer coordinates use cases, checking the shape of each incoming message, authorizing it, running the handler, and returning a result that carries no transport details. A use case is one command, which changes business state, or one query, which reads without changing state; a reaction answers an event without a request, and a job runs work on a schedule or by hand. This page states how use cases, reactions, and jobs are organized, what each stage of the command pipeline owns, and how ports and declared effects are wired.

pages.title: Backend Architecture
pages.intent: The backend is a modular monolith of four layers: Domain holds business rules, Application coordinates use cases, Infrastructure holds technical adapters, and WebApi holds HTTP transport. A use case is one command or query with its access, results, and scenarios, a reaction answers an event by running a command or sending a notification, and a job runs work on a schedule or by hand. This page states those layers, the direction their references point, and the module tree that organizes every layer; a team building the backend reads it before the layer pages, which state what each layer owns.

pages.title: Domain Layer
pages.intent: The Domain layer holds a product's business rules in code that depends on nothing but itself, so the rules are tested on their own. An aggregate is one unit of business state that stays consistent and changes in one step, and this page states how to model aggregates, their lifecycles, closed sets of values, and the domain repositories that load them. It also states the boundary that keeps technical concerns out of business rules.

pages.title: .NET HTTP API
pages.intent: Each HTTP operation in a .NET backend runs through one endpoint class in its use case folder, and the OpenAPI contract is generated from those classes at build time. This page states the endpoint contract, the metadata each operation declares, how transport models express closed sets, and how the global handler derives HTTP statuses from refusal codes. The shared transport rules live on [HTTP API](../api.md); this page holds only their .NET form.

pages.title: .NET Application Layer
pages.intent: Application code in a .NET backend sends commands and queries through mediators from LiteBus, the pinned messaging library: commands change business state, queries read without changing it, and validators report structural input problems as LiteBus validity values. This page binds that dispatch for .NET: the command-handler shape, the validity shape, the query-handler shape, the entry point for each declared effect, the use case folder layout, the pinned mediator methods, and the pinned pipeline bindings. The shared coordination rules live on [Application Layer](../application.md); this page holds only their .NET bindings.

pages.title: .NET Architecture
pages.intent: A .NET backend holds its business code in two projects, the shared kernel and the modules, with hosts that compose and serve them. This page binds that shape for .NET: which projects exist, how modules aggregates and use cases fill one namespace tree, which folders each level allows, and where host-only endpoints live, so every type keeps one home and boundaries hold by folder and mark. The shared architecture rules live on [Backend Architecture](../architecture.md); this page holds only their .NET bindings.

pages.title: .NET Configuration
pages.intent: A .NET backend pins its SDK, build settings, package versions, and local tools to fixed versions through files at fixed paths. This page states what each file sets, so every machine builds the same output. The shared configuration rules live on [Configuration](../../workspace/config.md); this page holds only their .NET form.

pages.title: .NET Domain Layer
pages.intent: Domain folders hold the business model of a .NET backend in C# types that depend on nothing but themselves, so no outer-layer concern leaks into business rules. An aggregate is one unit of business state that stays consistent and changes in one step, and this page states the C# shape of aggregates, their lifecycles and identities, child entities, value objects, closed sets, money, repositories, events, and the exceptions that reject broken rules. The shared domain rules live on [Domain Layer](../domain.md); each rule below cites the shared rule it realizes.

pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: The pages in this folder state the extensions only a .NET backend offers: executable acceptance scenarios and layer projects for backends that package each layer as its own project. A local extension stays inactive until one use case, journey, or module meets the criterion its page states; the project extension applies to the whole backend once selected. A use case is one command or query, a journey is the steps to one goal, and a module is one business area; authors turn to these pages when shared examples need business-language review, or when the backend keeps the five-project packaging.

pages.title: Executable BDD Acceptance Tests
pages.intent: This extension adds executable BDD scenarios for cross-layer examples that need review in business language and execution through a public boundary such as the HTTP API. Test authors write them as LightBDD feature classes, and use them for the critical examples its rules select, so product, domain, engineering, and testing discussions share one executable example. LightBDD binds steps at compile time, so a step that no longer exists, or whose parameters changed, fails the build rather than the run. Each BDD scenario proves one scenario record from the written specification, which stays the behavior source.

pages.title: Layer Projects
pages.intent: This extension packages each backend layer as its own .NET project: Domain, Application.Abstractions, Application, Infrastructure, and WebApi, with hosts beside them. It states the five-project form of the project, reference, package, and layout rules for backends already on five projects and for teams that want the compiler to hold Domain purity. The module layout is the default; this page holds the packaging that replaces it.

pages.title: .NET Naming and Code Style
pages.intent: C# code in a .NET backend names its files and implementation shapes one way across every project. This page states those .NET rules: one primary type per file, a shared implementation style, and names that state their reason. The shared naming rules live on [Naming and Code Style](../../workspace/naming.md); this page holds only their .NET form.

pages.title: .NET Packages
pages.intent: A .NET backend references only the LiteBus modules its code dispatches and reports .NET breaches in the editor and the build. This page states that module scope and the analyzer setup that reports each breach at the line that breaks it. The shared dependency rules live on [Dependencies](../../workspace/dependencies.md); this page holds only their .NET form.

pages.title: .NET Persistence
pages.intent: A .NET backend persists aggregates through Marten, the baseline document store: command handlers stage writes through Domain repositories, queries project through the read session, and one post-handler commits each command pipeline. This page states those .NET bindings with the Infrastructure folder layout and session lifetime they assume, so every command keeps one transaction. The shared persistence rules live on [Persistence](../persistence.md).

pages.title: .NET Stack
pages.intent: A backend built on .NET declares the `dotnet` stack in `.litespec/project.yaml`. The declaration applies every page in this folder, and it tells the model builder to read C# code and test results in TRX or JUnit XML. This page states the declaration, the form each mark takes in C#, the runtime values generated from the records, what the stack reader reads from C# code, the result formats the builder reads, and the test projects, packages, and runners.

pages.title: .NET Workspace
pages.intent: A .NET backend lives under `apps/api/`, with the solution beside its projects. This page states that .NET layout: the workspace solution and where the AppHost lives, so every file has one fixed address. The shared workspace rules live on [Workspace Structure](../../workspace/structure.md); this page holds only their .NET form.

pages.title: Persistence
pages.intent: Commands change aggregates and queries read them, with neither touching the database directly: repositories stage writes, the read session serves queries, and one post-handler commits each command. This page states that boundary, the transaction shape, and the obligations on stored data. One explicit boundary keeps storage decisions reviewable in Infrastructure instead of scattered through handlers.

pages.title: Backend Testing
pages.intent: Backend tests prove behavior at separate boundaries: domain logic with no dependencies, use-case coordination through the project's own handlers, real persistence and HTTP behavior through the production host, and structural rules with architecture tests. This page states which suites each project size keeps and what each suite runs with, while the [Testing](../quality/testing.md) quality page states the cross-stack proof rules. Separate boundaries keep fast tests fast and point each failure at the layer that broke.

pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: The Core pages state what every LiteSpec project shares: the principles, the record layers, the records that hold intent and behavior, and the rules for agents, writing, and releases. Read them in the order below when starting a project, then load only the pages each task touches.

pages.title: Access
pages.intent: Who may act in the product and how they reach it: actors, roles, permissions, the access each use case declares, entry points, and external systems. Actors and roles live in Intent as product decisions users see; permissions, entry points, and external systems live in Behavior as access design. The [use-cases page](use-cases.md) states the use cases that carry access, and the [model page](model.md) states the shared record rules.

pages.title: Agent Operating Protocol
pages.intent: An agent is software that reads task context, edits files, and runs checks. This page states the operating rules for an agent working in a LiteSpec project: which records of decided intent to read before editing, which provisions govern each change, which guidance wins when pages overlap, and which changes need the task authorizer before the agent acts. Following them keeps each run inside its authorized scope, preserves unrelated work, and ends it with a report the owner can check.

pages.title: Authoring Standard
pages.intent: Every page in LiteSpec shares one shape: a fixed style, testable rules called provisions, stable identifiers for those rules, and a table naming the evidence each rule needs. This page states that shape, the prose rules the validators enforce on LiteSpec's own pages, and how each release carries the complete contract. The [Project Model](model.md) and [Record Language](language.md) pages state the rules for the records a project writes, and one shared shape lets readers learn pages once.

pages.title: Automation
pages.intent: Automation states the work that runs without a request: the reactions answering events and the jobs running on schedule, once, or by hand. Agents write these records from Intent, and code carries them. The [Behavior overview](behavior.md) maps the five Behavior pages, and the [record language page](language.md) states how each field, value and record name is written.

pages.title: Behavior Records
pages.intent: Behavior states how the system acts to keep the promises Intent records: the words it uses, the areas it divides into, the things it keeps consistent, the rules that hold, and the behavior it defines with its endings and examples. Agents write these records from Intent, and code carries them. The [model page](model.md) states the shared record rules, the [intent page](intent.md) states the promises Behavior answers to, and the [record language page](language.md) states how each field, value and record name is written.

pages.title: Departures
pages.intent: A departure is the one record that sets a provision, a page or a finding code aside for one project, with its reason. This page states what a departure holds, when to record one, how it covers a finding, what no departure covers, and when it expires. The [model page](model.md) states the record types and the checks, and the [scope page](scope.md) states the record layers a project claims.

pages.title: Domain Model
pages.intent: Domain Model states the words and things inside the bounded context: the modules, the glossary, the aggregates with their lifecycles, the rules that hold, and the domain events. Agents write these records from Intent, and code carries them. The [Behavior overview](behavior.md) maps the five Behavior pages, and the [record language page](language.md) states how each field, value and record name is written.

pages.title: Edges and Screens
pages.intent: Edges and Screens states how the product meets the outside: the integration events, notifications, entry points, screens, and external systems. Agents write these records from Intent, and code carries them. The [Behavior overview](behavior.md) maps the five Behavior pages, and the [record language page](language.md) states how each field, value and record name is written.

pages.title: Intent Layer
pages.intent: Intent is why the product exists and what it promises: the product, its modules, actors, goals, problems, features with their requirements, journeys, constraints, research, decisions, and terms. This page states where Intent lives, what shape each record takes, and what Intent never holds, before Behavior states how the system keeps the promises. The [record language page](language.md) states how each field, value and record name is written.

pages.title: Record Language
pages.intent: Record Language states one grammar and one tone for every name, every identifier and every value a project writes or a tool prints. Agents and authors apply it to record fields, values, identifiers, finding codes and tool names. The [Authoring Standard](authoring.md) states the prose of LiteSpec pages, and the [Writing Standard](writing.md) states the prose of project records, explanation files and documents; this page states the names, values, identifiers and codes of project records.

pages.title: Record Layers
pages.intent: LiteSpec records form four record layers: Intent states the promises, Behavior states how the system keeps them, Implementation builds that behavior in code, and Proof shows that it holds. This page states the translation rules between the record layers: Specify, Implement, and Verify. Agents apply it at every record-layer boundary, and readers use it to judge whether each record layer says only what belongs to it.

pages.title: Maintaining the Standards
pages.intent: LiteSpec publishes each release as one complete contract, so the repository holding the standard needs its own operating rules. This page states them: how a provision, one identified obligation on a page, moves from draft to active to retired, how a rename replaces every citation of the old name in one change, and how a maintainer publishes a release from a git tag. The rules keep every provision identifier resolvable and every release reproducible from its tag.

pages.title: Project Model
pages.intent: A LiteSpec project describes itself with records, written statements of fixed types joined by fixed links. This page states the four record layers, the record types with their placement and identifiers, the record files, the explanation files, the documents, the common fields, the links, the marks, the authority order, the authoring order, the completion stages, the screen captures, the model builder, the check levels, and the book. People write Intent, agents write Behavior from it, and the model builder computes how code and tests connect to the records.

pages.title: Principles
pages.intent: These principles settle a design choice when no narrower provision prefers one design. LiteSpec defines a strict specification model of linked records beside graded engineering provisions, with git as the decision record. Apply this page when two designs both satisfy the narrower pages, and read the [layers page](layers.md) for the boundaries these principles govern.

pages.title: Privacy and Retention
pages.intent: Privacy and Retention states how the product handles personal data: the data classes with their erasure positions, the retention schedule, and the extended erasure needs of referenced rows, child rows, handed-over data, requested reach, export guards, conflicts, and restore sweeps. Agents write these records from Intent, and code carries them. The [Behavior overview](behavior.md) maps the five Behavior pages, and the [record language page](language.md) states how each field, value and record name is written.

pages.title: Product Release
pages.intent: A product release is the verified behavior a team ships as one immutable artifact. Teams apply this page at every release to run the checks their boundaries select, to read completion computed from proof, and to write the release record and the verification report. A project that selects the [Delivery extension](../ext/delivery.md) adds its deployment and rollback rules on top.

pages.title: Supported Scope
pages.intent: LiteSpec is a standard for specification-driven development of one bounded-context business application by people and coding agents. This page states what each project choice decides, which extensions and outside constraints the project also declares, what claiming conformance means, and where the supported boundary ends. A team declares them once during inception, before writing anything else down, so agents and checks apply exactly the pages the project selected.

pages.title: Provision Scopes
pages.intent: Provisions are filed by concern: each page states the rules for one concern, while an agent changing one file needs every rule for that situation. This page states the shared situation vocabulary each provision carries: its stack, its concern, its artifact, the record layer it governs, its trace, and its strength. Authors write these values when they write or grade a provision, and the provision index carries them so the CLI lists the provisions that apply to one path and the record layer each provision belongs to.

pages.title: Technology Stacks
pages.intent: A stack binds the specification to one technology: a backend stack lives under `backend/`, a frontend stack under `frontend/`. Selecting one applies exactly the provisions, version pins, and checks that technology needs. This page states what selecting a stack applies, where its versions come from, and how a replacement names every baseline provision it replaces.

pages.title: LiteSpec
pages.intent: LiteSpec is a system for building software from written records: the records state the required behavior, and people and agents build, verify, and operate against them. This page states what that system is and which parts it combines, while the intent, behavior, access, layers, and model pages state the records and the rules between them. A team starting a project reads it first, so every later choice lands in one shared model joining intent to code.

pages.title: Use Cases
pages.intent: Use Cases states what the system does and what it answers: the commands and queries, their verbs, inputs, effects, endings, scenarios, and the settings they read. Agents write these records from Intent, and code carries them. The [Behavior overview](behavior.md) maps the five Behavior pages, and the [record language page](language.md) states how each field, value and record name is written.

pages.title: Writing
pages.intent: Writing states how every project writes its records, explanation files and documentation pages, so a reader who arrives cold on one page still learns who acts, what is at stake and what holds. Authors and agents apply it to every record value, explanation file, document, code comment, changelog and decision record. The [Record Language](language.md) page states the names, values and codes of project records; this page states the prose.

pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: The example pages show LiteSpec applied to one product, Claimwick, a small application in which employees submit work expenses with receipts, managers approve or refuse them, and finance reimburses the approved ones. Its records live in `examples/claimwick/.litespec/`, and its code, screen and tests sit beside them in the same repository. Every record ID, file path, count and command output on these pages is copied from that repository or from a real run of `litespec` against it, so a reader can open the same file and see the same text. The pages state no rules of their own: each rule lives on the standards page that the text cites.

pages.title: The Claimwick Product
pages.intent: Claimwick is the product this example follows: employees submit work expenses with receipts, managers approve or refuse them, and finance reimburses the approved ones. This page shows its Intent records as they are written in `examples/claimwick/.litespec/intent/`, from the product brief down to the journey that ties them together. Every record, field, ID and count below is copied from that folder, so a reader can open the same file and see the same text.

pages.title: Modules and Records
pages.intent: The Spending module turns the Intent of [The Claimwick Product](the-product.md) into Behavior: the aggregates that hold each expense, policy and receipt, the rules that guard them, the use cases that change them, and the entry point, screen, reaction, job, notification and setting around them. This page lists those records as they are written in `examples/claimwick/.litespec/behavior/modules/spending/`, with the counts and IDs a reader can check in the folder.
sections: The Entry Point and the Screen
The Reaction, Job, Notification and Settings
The Permissions and the Access Chain

pages.title: A Use Case in Code
pages.intent: This page follows one use case, Submit expense, from its record into the .NET code and the acceptance tests that prove it. The record is `examples/claimwick/.litespec/behavior/modules/spending/expenses/submit-expense.yaml`, and the code and tests are in `examples/claimwick/apps/api/`. Every file path and line of code below is copied from that folder, so a reader can check the chain from record to test in one sitting.

pages.title: The Claimwick Screen
pages.intent: The expenses screen is the one screen of Claimwick's web app that the example builds. It shows an employee their own expenses at the address `/expenses`. This page follows that screen from its route file, through the generated API client it reads, the shared UI package it composes, and the pattern catalog that records its interface choices, with the file of each step and the check the model runs over it.

pages.title: The Model and Its Checks
pages.intent: The project model joins the written records of a project to its code, screens and tests, and its checks report every gap as a finding. This page shows those checks on Claimwick with real output: the full run of `litespec model check` on the example, the departures that cover its 26 findings, and the record and query commands an agent uses to load one record. Each command below was run against `examples/claimwick`, and the output is copied from that run.
