pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: The extensions pages hold conditional provision bundles a project adds only when a specific need appears, from caching and audit trails to multitenancy and delivery, so a project carries no provision it does not need. Each bundle stays inactive until a current need meets the criterion its page states, and the project records each choice with its criterion. A team facing a need the default provisions do not cover reads the candidate page and selects only the extensions whose criteria hold today.

pages.title: AI Assistance
pages.intent: Some queries are answered through a model that picks tools to gather facts and compose the answer. This page states the closed tool set, the structure-only scenarios, the pinned stub, and the provenance those queries carry. A project selects it for each query a model mediates.

pages.title: Audit Trail
pages.intent: An audit trail proves who attempted what inside data one party owns while another party acts in it, including attempts the system refused. This page states what the trail stores for each attempt, which attempts it covers, where the producer runs, how the store resists tampering, and how a reviewer reads the trail. A team whose system acts in another party's data selects this extension and keeps one trail that proves accountability instead of reconstructing the answer from logs and domain events (facts the system recorded as completed).

pages.title: Caching
pages.intent: A cache answers repeated expensive reads from stored results instead of recomputing them, trading lower latency and source load for stale reads and invalidation work. This page states when that trade is justified, what each cache's staleness contract covers, how keys separate results, and how the system behaves when the cache fails. A team applies it once traces or load tests name a repeated expensive read, so each cache carries a staleness bound the team chose instead of one it discovers during an incident.

pages.title: API Compatibility
pages.intent: API compatibility keeps consumers that release on their own schedule working when the API or its published events change, including public, partner, and mobile clients. This page states how a project classifies each contract and event change, versions breaking ones, keeps supported versions alive, and retires them with notice. A team with such consumers applies it, so its consumers keep working across releases instead of breaking on deploy day.

pages.title: Concurrency and Idempotency
pages.intent: Concurrency and idempotency rules stop overlapping writes from silently overwriting each other and stop a retried request from executing twice. This page states how a project documents conflicting writes, coordinates them with versions, and makes retried operations return one result through client keys and fingerprints. A team applies it when overlap or retry can corrupt behavior, so its callers get one predictable outcome instead of a silent overwrite or a duplicated effect.

pages.title: Customer Rules and Hooks
pages.intent: Some products let customers build their own rules from triggers, conditions, and actions, and call customer endpoints when those rules fire. This page states the catalog those rules draw from, the tenant instances as data, and the may and may-not contract on hooks. A project selects it when tenants compose customer rules or the product calls customer hooks.

pages.title: Delivery
pages.intent: Delivery holds the release, deployment and operations rules a project adds when running the product for other people takes a formal regime: release readiness gates, artifact promotion, deployment and rollback, backup and restore, alerts and runbooks, the supply-chain gate, container image build, rollout and runtime limits, and agent handoff. A project that only needs the core checks, contracts and review flow in the baseline carries none of it. A team that operates the product in production selects it, so each release deploys, recovers and answers alerts by a written procedure instead of improvisation, with container releases shipping the same image bytes they tested.

pages.title: Connected Devices
pages.intent: Devices hold state, apply rules, and sync while offline, so the product owes them a protocol: messages, versions, client rules, and the shape of offline uploads. This page states the `protocol` block an entry point carries when devices reach it. A project selects it for each entry point that serves scanners, kiosks, or offline-capable clients.

pages.title: External Integrations
pages.intent: External integrations connect the product to providers it does not control, which can fail, change their responses, or deliver one message twice. This page states how a use case (one command or query the product offers) names the outside behavior it needs, where provider details live, how failures map to project-owned results with stable refusal codes, and how tests simulate the network boundary. A team applies it for each use case that calls a provider, receives a webhook, or imports provider-shaped data, so a provider change touches one folder instead of the whole codebase.

pages.title: Jobs and Queues
pages.intent: Work that outlives a request runs in a Worker: scheduled jobs from a timetable and reports too heavy for a request, while people clear queued items through claimed listings. This page states how each kind records its work, runs it once, and recovers. A project selects it for recurring, delayed, heavy, or human-cleared work.

pages.title: Data Lifecycle
pages.intent: Data lifecycle rules decide how long each piece of stored data lives: how long it stays, when it is deleted, and when it can return. This page states what the team writes down for each lifetime and which behavior the code owns: hard delete wherever nothing needs the data later, explicit archive and restore states where a use case (one command or query the product offers) needs them, and authorized, audited operations throughout. A team selects it for each use case or rule that deletes, retains, archives, restores, holds, exports, or reuses data after deletion, so no data lingers past its retention and no deletion breaks a legal or business duty.

pages.title: Localization
pages.intent: Localization makes every screen, message, route, and formatted value answer to the user's language. This page states what the team decides up front, the supported locales, the default locale, the fallback chain, and the route shape, and which behavior the code owns: catalogs for copy, locale-aware formatting, and business data that stays locale-neutral. A project selects it when it ships in more than one locale, so each language reads as a complete product instead of a partial translation.

pages.title: Model Context Protocol
pages.intent: A Model Context Protocol server lets a large language model (LLM) client on the user's own machine call the product's public API. This page states how that server presents itself, describes its tools, and words its refusals; the API pages own the behavior the server calls. A project selects it when it ships such a server, so the model plans from accurate tool descriptions and every write waits for the person's confirmation.

pages.title: Durable Delivery
pages.intent: Committed changes reach the outside world through durable delivery that survives crashes. This page states how the product stages after-commit effects in the outbox for a Worker to deliver. A team selects it for delivery that survives process failure.

pages.title: Plans and Entitlements
pages.intent: A product that gates behavior and amounts by tier records each plan's entitlements in one place: the behavior the plan unlocks and the amounts it allows. This page states how the product records its plans, how behavior and amounts resolve to what the acting plan entitles, and how the product answers a run past its plan. A project selects it when tiers change what the software allows, so a plan change moves one record instead of scattered checks.

pages.title: Live Delivery
pages.intent: Live updates reach open screens in seconds through a realtime transport the browser keeps open. This page states when the product replaces polling with realtime transport, which transport carries each kind of live update, and how connections, subscriptions, and clients stay safe under load and failure. A team selects it after it measures polling against an update target and accepts the cost of disconnects and missed messages.

pages.title: Release Stage
pages.intent: The release stage tells whether any deployment holds customer data yet, because several provisions assume a running service that the first builds do not have. This page states how a project declares its stage, which provisions the early stage defers and until when, and how a recorded decision ends the deferral. A project selects it while no deployment holds customer data, or afterwards to record a past move to production, so relaxed early provisions expire on a date instead of lingering by accident.

pages.title: Multitenancy
pages.intent: Multitenancy lets independent customer organizations share one deployment while each keeps isolated data and policy. This page states how the product resolves tenant identity from trusted context, isolates each tenant's data and policy across authorization, storage, caches, reactions, jobs, exports, diagnostics, and recovery, and records the operations that cross tenant lines. A project selects it when separate customers require isolated data or policy in one deployment, because a tenant column without these obligations leaks one customer's data to another.

pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: The frontend pages state how the browser and device side of a LiteSpec product is built: its frame, routes, and modules named for the backend use cases they call, the shared components and governed visual language, the interface pattern catalog, and how data, rendering, and testing work, with the bindings each stack realizes. Frontend teams and agents follow them when they add a route, build a screen, or change shared UI or data code, so every screen answers the same question the same way.

pages.title: Blazor Stack
pages.intent: The Blazor stack is the technology binding for a product that has no server of its own: a .NET domain model, browser-local persistence, and a Blazor WebAssembly application compiled to static files. A team chooses it when the product runs entirely on the user's device, under the `client-only` shape declared in [Supported Scope](../../core/scope.md). This frontend sits outside the controlled UI contract, which covers React and Svelte only, so its entry point record names the boundaries that replace that contract.

pages.title: Frontend Components
pages.intent: Every screen in a LiteSpec frontend draws with components from one shared UI package: small primitives such as inputs and badges, and larger composites such as sections and tables built from them. This page states what that package holds, how page code, the components under each route or module folder, composes its parts, and where a drawing that no composite makes belongs. Frontend developers and coding agents apply it whenever they build or change a screen, so the product keeps one visual language and a restyle stays a change in one place.

pages.title: Frontend Data and State
pages.intent: A LiteSpec frontend owns no API contract: it calls the API through one generated client, reads answers through the client's cache, and sends each write as a command, one message that changes business state. This page states how the client is built and configured, where each piece of state lives, and how every failure reaches the user as one problem, a project-owned failure shape carrying a stable code. Frontend developers and agents apply it for every read, write, and form, so a contract change breaks the build instead of the running page and every failure renders a sentence the team wrote for it.

pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: The shared mobile pages state what every native mobile app does the same way: one .NET solution tree, native screens with one navigation controller, handlers with classified state, least-access device use, and core and device tests across structure, screens, data, device, and testing. No project selects this folder directly; selecting the [Android Stack](android/stack.md) applies it through that stack's folder chain. A developer or agent adding a screen, a device feature, or data code to a mobile app finds the shared rule here and the stack-specific rule on the stack page.

pages.title: Android Stack
pages.intent: The Android stack is the technology binding for a product that ships a native Android application built with .NET for Android in C# against plain Android views. A team chooses it with either shape, `client-only` or `server`, declared in [Supported Scope](../../../core/scope.md). This frontend sits outside the controlled UI contract, which covers React and Svelte only, so its entry point record names the boundaries that replace that contract.

pages.title: Mobile Data and State
pages.intent: Data handling in a mobile app routes every use case through an Application handler, the one place where that use case is defined. Every piece of state carries a declared classification deciding whether it is persisted, kept on the device, or recomputed. This page states the mobile store, storage, and client those rules land in, following [Frontend Data and State](../data.md) (`litespec/frontend/data#route-use-cases-through-application`, `litespec/frontend/data#classify-state`, `litespec/frontend/data#update-the-cache-a-command-changed`), and a team that applies it while writing handlers and screens keeps one definition of each use case and one source of each value.

pages.title: Mobile Device Capabilities
pages.intent: A mobile app borrows device capabilities: the camera roll, the microphone, the speaker, and the permissions guarding them. This page states how the app picks media, requests permissions, plays sound, and declares what it uses. A team that applies it while adding a device feature keeps the app asking for the least access and behaving while shared hardware is busy.

pages.title: Mobile Screens and Navigation
pages.intent: A mobile app renders its screens with the platform's native views, holds navigation in one controller, and follows the platform's back, inset, and motion behavior. This page states those screen and navigation rules for every mobile stack. A team that applies it while adding screens keeps navigation in one place and every screen behaving the way the platform's users expect.

pages.title: Mobile Structure
pages.intent: A mobile consumer holds its apps in one .NET solution whose core projects carry the domain model and whose platform projects carry the screens. This page states that solution tree, the projects each shape holds, and the screen folders, with the import direction between them following `litespec/frontend/structure#order-imports-from-routes-to-shared-packages`. A team that applies it while adding apps and screens keeps every platform sharing one core and every layer building only on the layers inside it.

pages.title: Mobile Testing
pages.intent: The mobile app proves its behavior at two boundaries: core tests without a device, and device tests that drive each screen on an emulator or device. This page states how it follows the testing principles in [Frontend Testing](../testing.md) and where each kind of test lives. A team that applies it while writing tests keeps fast tests fast and still proves every screen where users meet it.

pages.title: UI Patterns
pages.intent: One pattern catalog decides each recurring interface question once, such as how an expense page lays out or what an empty list shows, instead of letting each screen invent its own answer. This page states what each catalog entry holds: the options considered, the option chosen and who chose it, the narrow-screen behavior, and the implementation status per platform. Product owners and frontend teams use it when they choose and build interface behavior, so every screen answers the same question the same way instead of each route inventing its own answer.

pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: The pattern pages decide each recurring interface question once, as drawn options with a named default to build, so every screen answers the same question the same way. A team building a screen starts from the page for its question, an owner picks an option from the drawings, and the team records the choice in its pattern catalog. The [UI Patterns](../patterns.md) page states the catalog contract, the pattern layout, and the wireframe language these pages share.

pages.title: Admin Screen Patterns
pages.intent: Settings screens configure the company itself, and this page shows each screen as drawn options with a named default to build: the team and its roles, API keys and webhooks, data import, the payout account, subscription invoices, and budget limits and advances. The product owner chooses among the options when the team builds or revises a settings area. Consistent admin layouts keep powerful commands, such as granting access, rotating secrets, and paying invoices, safe to operate.

pages.title: Create, Edit and Remove Patterns
pages.intent: Staff create records such as expenses, trips, and fares, change them, and remove one or several, and this page shows the layout for each task as drawn options with a named default to build, including the special cases: draft-first creation, corrections to the past, duplicates, hand ordering, restoring archived work, invitations, publishing, and scheduled changes. The product owner chooses among the options when the team builds or revises a working screen. One decided shape per task keeps destructive and far-reaching commands predictable, so staff know what a command will do before they commit.

pages.title: Dialog and Overlay Patterns
pages.intent: A dialog, drawer, popover, menu, toast, context menu, shortcut overlay, bottom sheet, or persistent bar floats above or beside the page to confirm, edit, preview, or announce without a full navigation. This page shows when each overlay fits and how it opens, holds focus, and closes, as drawn options with a named default to build. The product owner chooses among the options when the team adds a confirmation, a side preview, or any floating layer. Right-sized overlays keep staff oriented: the page stays visible behind short tasks, and irreversible commands get the full attention they need.

pages.title: Feedback and State Patterns
pages.intent: This page holds the patterns for the states a screen shows around its work: no records yet, no results, loading, a refused command, a command that worked, a notice before acting, a forbidden page, no connection, an expired sign-in, a conflict, work that runs in the background, a missing record, a server failure, maintenance, and a rate limit. An owner picks an option from the drawings, and the team records the choice in its pattern catalog, the file holding the project's interface decisions. Each decided state says what happened, what it means, and what to do next, so staff never guess what a screen is telling them.

pages.title: Form and Field Patterns
pages.intent: This page holds the patterns for entering a value into a form, and for what the form reports around it: money, record pickers, dates, text, single choices, switches, uploads, refused submits, unsaved work, periods, slugs, capacity, colors, repeated groups, tags, addresses, and message templates. A team building a form starts from these patterns, an owner picks an option from the drawings, and the team records the choice in its pattern catalog, the file holding the project's interface decisions. One decided shape per field keeps entry fast and errors fixable, so staff type once and repair only what the message names.

pages.title: List and Table Patterns
pages.intent: This page holds the patterns for the expenses list, which shows many records of one kind so a reader can find one record, compare rows, and act on them: columns, sorting, filters, row density, selection, paging, row actions, table states, status, money, export, search, grouping, expansion, pinning, and the layout of a short list. A team building a list screen starts from these patterns, an owner picks an option from the drawings, and the team records the choice in its pattern catalog, the file holding the project's interface decisions. One shared set of answers keeps every list in the product behaving the same way, so a reader who learns one list knows them all.

pages.title: Money, Time and Density Patterns
pages.intent: This page holds the patterns for writing amounts, statements, moments, periods, counts, charts, payouts, invoices, VAT, and identifiers at every width, read across tables, statements, charts, and phone screens. A team building a finance or reporting screen starts from these patterns, an owner picks an option from the drawings, and the team records the choice in its pattern catalog, the file holding the project's interface decisions. One shared way of writing figures keeps exports, statements, and screens agreeing, so finance can cite a figure without checking where it was read.

pages.title: Navigation Patterns
pages.intent: This page holds the patterns for the product frame around every screen, which lets a reader move between areas and know where they are: sidebar, breadcrumb, header bar, tabs, icons, language and theme, command palette, account menu, notifications, help, and workspace switching. A team building the product frame starts from these patterns, an owner picks an option from the drawings, and the team records the choice in its pattern catalog, the file holding the project's interface decisions. One shared product frame keeps every page reachable by address and marked in place, so a reader never loses where they are.

pages.title: Page Frame Patterns
pages.intent: This page holds the layout pattern for each kind of page: home, list, queue, record, form, report, settings, editor, outcome, operations, schedule, setup, and error. A team building a new screen starts from these patterns, an owner picks an option from the drawings, and the team records the choice in its pattern catalog, the file holding the project's interface decisions. One layout per kind keeps every screen predictable, so a reader knows where the heading, actions, and content sit before reading.

pages.title: Record Detail Patterns
pages.intent: One screen shows one record of the product, with its state, facts, history, and the commands a reader may run, and this page holds the patterns for that screen: header, tabs, summary, aside, timeline, relations, refusals, change history, notes, attachments, identifiers, neighbor movement, and the whole record screen assembled from them. A team building a record screen starts from these patterns, an owner picks an option from the drawings, and the team records the choice in its pattern catalog, the file holding the project's interface decisions. One shared record shape keeps every record readable in the same order, so support finds the state and the next step without hunting.

pages.title: Frontend Rendering and Routes
pages.intent: A route answers three questions: which web address it serves, which data it needs, and which floorplan, the page component fixing the page layout, draws it. This page states how a route loads its data before rendering, how the address carries its parameters, how routes and languages load separately, and how each route state renders. Frontend developers and agents apply it for every address the product serves, so each page renders with its data in place and no route shows a blank region where a request is pending or failed.

pages.title: Frontend Structure
pages.intent: A LiteSpec frontend holds three parts: a frame holding what every route shares, routes for the addresses it serves, and one module folder per backend use case it calls, with the module tree mirroring the backend module folders in kebab case. This page states those parts, the import direction between them, and where a file shared by several use cases belongs. Frontend developers and agents apply it whenever they add or move frontend code, so a reader holding a use-case specification finds the frontend code that serves it without a second map.

pages.title: Frontend Testing
pages.intent: Frontend tests prove behavior at the cheapest level that represents the risk: unit tests for pure logic, browser suites against a running deployment for navigation and integration, and one route check for every address. This page states which kind proves what, how a test proves a use case by calling it and asserting the result each scenario names, and where mocks may stand. Frontend developers and agents apply it whenever they add or change a test, so each risk is proved once at the right level instead of slowly everywhere or nowhere at all.

pages.title: Controlled UI Governance
pages.intent: The shared UI package is a constrained construction language: the ready-made controls, the interaction behavior, the page layouts, and the named visual values every screen draws with. This page states how the workspace governs that language: the visual authority, the design contract, the floorplan set, and the route suite that proves every route. Frontend teams and agents apply it whenever they add or change a screen, a component, or a named value, so every page of one kind looks and behaves as one page.

pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: The web pages state what the React and Svelte frontends do the same way: one TypeScript toolchain, one generated API client, and one shared UI package across structure, rendering, components, UI, data, and testing. No project selects this folder directly; selecting the [React Stack](react/stack.md) or [Svelte Stack](svelte/stack.md) applies it through that stack's folder chain. A developer or agent adding a route, a component, or data code to a React or Svelte frontend finds the shared rule here and the stack-specific rule on the stack page.

pages.title: TypeScript Web Components
pages.intent: Every screen in a TypeScript web frontend draws with composites, shared building blocks for layout and interaction, from one shared UI package, instead of each application drawing its own. The component principles live in [Frontend Components](../components.md); this page states the TypeScript mechanism behind them for the [React Stack](react/stack.md) and [Svelte Stack](svelte/stack.md): the registry source holding the primitives every composite builds on, the closed list of refused raw elements, visual files for drawings no composite makes, the raw HTML sinks kept away from untrusted content, the typed component boundaries, and the route checks both stacks share. A team that applies it while writing pages keeps layout and interaction inside governed composites instead of scattered raw elements.

pages.title: Web Data and State
pages.intent: The frontend keeps no copy of the API contract: it generates its client, types, schemas, and query options from the published OpenAPI document. The data rules live in [Frontend Data and State](../data.md); this page holds the TypeScript mechanism behind them that the [React Stack](react/stack.md) and [Svelte Stack](svelte/stack.md) share. A team that applies it while writing data code keeps every application consistent with the contract and every failure recoverable by the reader.

pages.title: Web UI Patterns
pages.intent: The web mechanism for UI patterns lives in [Web UI](ui.md), which states the pattern implementation for the [React Stack](react/stack.md) and [Svelte Stack](svelte/stack.md) together with the other shared UI rules. A reader looking for the web implementation of a chosen pattern finds it there.

pages.title: React Stack
pages.intent: A React frontend takes one of three rendering modes, chosen by who reads it: a static application for an authenticated console, server rendering for a public surface a user reaches by link or search, and one static page with no router for a device client. A team opening a React frontend chooses the mode under [Web Rendering](../rendering.md) before writing routes, and finds on this page the names, files, and libraries the shared web pages leave to this stack. The shared stack rules in [Technology Stacks](../../../core/stacks.md) apply to every stack.

pages.title: Web Rendering and Routes
pages.intent: A route in a TypeScript web frontend carries metadata deciding how links and search meet it. This page states the metadata rule the [React Stack](react/stack.md) and [Svelte Stack](svelte/stack.md) add to the rendering rules in [Frontend Rendering and Routes](../rendering.md). A team that applies it while writing routes keeps every public route linkable and every private route out of search.

pages.title: Web Structure
pages.intent: React and Svelte frontends share one folder layout: a frame holding the values shared across routes, one route per address, and modules that mirror the backend's use cases so each business area and user task sits in the same place on both sides. This page states the tree, the frame folder, the use-case marks, the generated records file, and the route tree the [React Stack](react/stack.md) and [Svelte Stack](svelte/stack.md) share, following the structure rules in [Frontend Structure](../structure.md). A team that applies it while adding files keeps every use case findable by path and every mark checkable by type.

pages.title: Svelte Stack
pages.intent: A Svelte frontend takes one of three rendering modes, chosen by who reads it: a static SvelteKit application for an authenticated console, server rendering for a public surface a user reaches by link or search, and one static page with no router for a device client. A team opening a Svelte frontend chooses the mode under [Web Rendering](../rendering.md) before writing routes, and finds on this page the names, files, and libraries the shared web pages leave to this stack. The shared stack rules in [Technology Stacks](../../../core/stacks.md) apply to every stack.

pages.title: Web Testing
pages.intent: Web frontends prove pure logic in Vitest beside the module it covers and navigation and integration in Playwright against the running system. The testing principles live in [Frontend Testing](../testing.md); this page names the runners, libraries, and commands one web frontend uses for them, and refuses a test with no assertion. A team that applies it while writing tests keeps fast tests fast and proves every address and every declared refusal, each named way a use case, one user task, says no, in a browser.

pages.title: Web UI
pages.intent: One shared UI package carries the pieces every route composes: the registry of page references, the token stylesheet, and the baseline source it installs once. This page states the registry build, the suite marks, the CSS decisions, and the source rules one web frontend requires, following the UI rules in [Controlled UI Governance](../ui.md). A team that applies it while writing shared UI keeps every registry item buildable, every suite marked with what it proves, and every primitive traceable to its source.

pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: The Guides section teaches by doing: tutorials take a reader to a first working result one step at a time, and how-to guides solve one stated problem in a project that already runs. Every guide cites the standard it applies and adds no rule of its own, so a reader learns the standard by following along.

pages.title: Add a Blazor Frontend
pages.intent: A product that serves its interface from Blazor runs as a client with no server of its own, with the domain model, handlers, and pages in one Blazor WebAssembly application. Blazor stays outside the controlled UI contract, so no floorplan or baseline step applies. This guide declares that frontend for a `client-only` project: the stack, the project shape, and the feature layout. Each step names the standard it satisfies, and the guide adds no rule of its own.

pages.title: Add a Stack or an Extension
pages.intent: A LiteSpec maintainer adds a stack or an extension so the release can name it in `litespec.manifest.yaml` and apply its pages. This guide moves the add-a-stack and add-an-extension procedures into the Maintain section. It adds no rule of its own.

pages.title: Add a Svelte Frontend
pages.intent: A product that serves its web interface from Svelte declares the same web application tree as the React frontend in the tutorial, against the same backend use cases. This guide declares that frontend: the stack, the application tree with mirrored use case paths, routes composed from one floorplan, and the pinned baseline. Each step names the standard it satisfies, and the guide adds no rule of its own.

pages.title: Add an Android Frontend
pages.intent: A product that serves its interface from Android declares a mobile solution with screens organized by module and hosted in one activity. Android stays outside the controlled UI contract, so no floorplan or baseline step applies. This guide declares that frontend: the stack, the mobile solution tree, and the screen layout. Each step names the standard it satisfies, and the guide adds no rule of its own.

pages.title: Build an Audit Trail
pages.intent: An audit trail proves who attempted what against which data and what each attempt produced, so a product can answer for every sensitive action. This guide builds that proof on the LiteBus pipeline that runs each state change in the .NET backend: the entry shape, the pipeline handlers, the protected store, and the read path. Each step names the audit rule it satisfies, and the guide adds no rule of its own.

pages.title: Folder Reference
pages.intent: Every record has exactly one parent, and its folder states that parent: the product, a module, an aggregate, or an entry point. This guide lists the one folder each record type lives in, the parent each folder stands for, and the qualified identifier the tool computes from the placement. Each step names the standard it satisfies, and the guide adds no rule of its own.

pages.title: Install the CLI
pages.intent: Each LiteSpec release ships the `litespec` command line in two forms: the `LiteSpec.Cli` .NET tool on nuget.org, and a standalone archive per platform on the [GitHub release](https://github.com/Litenova-Solutions/LiteSpec/releases). Both hold the same native executable, compiled ahead of time for the platform, and both carry the LiteSpec release beside it, so the executable needs no .NET runtime and no network. This guide installs the command line for a consumer repository or a machine, checks the download, and runs it in continuous integration. It adds no rule of its own.

pages.title: Start with Records Only
pages.intent: A team that wants LiteSpec's records, book and checks before it changes any code follows this guide. It claims `intent` and `behavior` in the project file, writes the first Intent and Behavior records, and runs the model check and the book, while its code and tests keep their own layout and practice. The [adoption page](../learn/adopting-litespec.md) states the claims that come next, `implementation` and `proof`.

pages.title: Write a Feature Under a Module
pages.intent: A feature is one answer to a problem under a module, advancing a goal and solving that problem, and it lives under the module that holds the problem: one file at `.litespec/intent/modules/<module>/features/<feature>.yaml` carrying the feature with its requirements as entries. This guide writes that file: the offering, the links to the problem and the goal, one requirement entry per commitment, and the explanation file beside it. Each step names the standard it satisfies, and the guide adds no rule of its own.

pages.title: Write Code for a Use Case
pages.intent: A use case is one command or query with its access, results, and scenarios, and its code spreads across every backend layer. This guide places each code element of a use case in its folder and gives it the mark its record needs, so a writer adds a use case without hunting six pages.

pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: The Intent records hold the research and decisions behind LiteSpec's provisions, in the shapes a consumer uses. They inform the provisions and settle nothing themselves: the provision remains the only obligation, and these records are never selected or applied as contract.

pages.title: One Grammar for Names and Values
Overview
pages.intent: The Learn pages explain LiteSpec, the standard for building one business application from written rules that tools check, to a reader who is new to it: the problem it solves, how its parts fit, how to read the standard, and how a team adopts it. They apply to every project and role, and they state no rules of their own: each rule lives on the standards page they link to. Technical leads and developers read them in order below when they evaluate or adopt LiteSpec, before opening any rules page.

pages.title: Why LiteSpec Exists
pages.intent: LiteSpec exists because teams that build with AI agents watch the same request produce a different design each time, while the reasons behind past designs leave with the people who made them. This page names those failure modes and the 3 parts LiteSpec answers with: a versioned standard (one published set of rules), written records (short YAML files stating product intent), and a model builder (the command joining records to code, screens, and tests) that checks one against the other. Technical leads read it when they decide whether LiteSpec fits their team.

pages.title: How LiteSpec Works
pages.intent: LiteSpec connects what a team writes about a product to the code that implements it, and checks that the two still agree. This page explains the parts, the record layers and the tools, then follows one use case of Claimwick, the example product in `examples/claimwick/`, from its written record to the check that confirms it. The worked example is in [The Claimwick Product](../example/the-product.md) and the pages after it.
sections: A Use Case from Record to Code

pages.title: Read the Standard
pages.intent: A LiteSpec project chooses a selection (its size, shape, technology stacks, extensions, and the record layers it claims, recorded in the project file `.litespec/project.yaml`) and applies only the pages that selection names, because the standard is large and most of it never applies to one project. This page explains those choices, the folder arrangement they select from, the anatomy of a rules page, and the departures the standard provides for rules a project cannot follow.

pages.title: Reading Tracks
pages.intent: A specification is a tree, and no reader reads the whole tree at once. This page states the order to read in: why before how, one journey from goal to proof, one module from aggregates to proof, and the structural words every record uses. Readers take it after [How LiteSpec Works](how-litespec-works.md), before they open their first record.

pages.title: How LiteSpec Compares
pages.intent: LiteSpec is one of many ways to specify work for AI coding agents, beside per-feature workflows, standards systems, instruction files, and tests. This page compares LiteSpec with 14 other approaches on the same dimensions: what each one specifies, how its rules are checked, and how it fits beside LiteSpec. Technical leads read it while they evaluate options, so they can place LiteSpec correctly instead of treating every approach as a rival.

pages.title: Lineage
pages.intent: LiteSpec borrows its words from established practices: each borrowed concept keeps its source's name, so a reader who knows the source already knows the word. This page names each practice, what LiteSpec takes from it, the words it uses, and what LiteSpec does differently. New readers take it after [How LiteSpec Compares](how-litespec-compares.md), as background rather than rules.
sections: Impact Mapping and Jobs to Be Done

pages.title: Work with Agents
pages.intent: An AI coding agent (software that reads task context, changes files, and runs checks) does its best work when the rules are written down and the checks run before review. This page explains how an agent finds the LiteSpec rules for your project, the order it follows on a task, and which decisions stay with you. Team members read it when they first hand work to an agent, so the agent starts from your records instead of its own habits.
sections: Agent Decisions and the Closed Specification

pages.title: Adopt LiteSpec in Steps
pages.intent: Adopting LiteSpec means pinning one release, claiming the record layers the team uses, and building to those claims with their checks in place. A team starts with Intent and Behavior, adds Implementation and Proof when it is ready, and works in either order. Each departure from a single provision stays recorded until it is resolved.

pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: The Maintain section documents the `litespec-maintain` command line: the three commands that keep the LiteSpec standard itself consistent, from authoring checks to the generated provision index and the release changelog. A maintainer opens this index to find the command that checks, rebuilds, or compares the standard. On a command page, Name and Synopsis give the quick form, and Description and Examples give the detail.

pages.title: Generate Provision Changelog
pages.intent: `litespec-maintain changelog` writes the provision changes since a git ref into the changelog.

pages.title: Generate Provisions
pages.intent: `litespec-maintain provisions` writes the provision index and its data file, resolving every identifier to its page, record layer, trace, and checked share, and writes the finding code table, the record folder table, and the manifest pin table.

pages.title: Validate Standards
pages.intent: `litespec-maintain validate` checks the LiteSpec repository against its own authoring contract.

pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: The Quality pages state what a release proves beyond its behavior: who may act and what happens to sensitive data, how the product runs, which checks each pull request runs, and how each scenario is proved. Each page applies to a project that claims the record layer its rules govern, as the layer table below states. A project that operates in production adds the [Delivery extension](../ext/delivery.md) for its release gate, deployment, recovery and alerting regime.

pages.title: Continuous Integration
pages.intent: Every pull request runs a fixed set of CI jobs, and each job checks one surface: compilation, tests, measured checks, the project model of records joined to code, documentation, and generated contracts. This page names those jobs and states which file changes select each one. No change merges with its surface unchecked; mutation testing, the supply-chain gate, artifact promotion, branch protection and the release job live in the [Delivery extension](../ext/delivery.md) for projects that select it.

pages.title: Operations
pages.intent: Operating a product means starting it, watching it, and keeping its runtime state visible, and this page states how a LiteSpec product does each: local startup, diagnostics, and the operating records that answer failures. It applies to everyone who operates a release and to any change that touches schema, external dependencies, or background work. A product that follows it stays observable with one maintainer on call; deployment, rollback, backup, restore, alerts, runbooks and the alerting regime live in the [Delivery extension](../ext/delivery.md) for projects that select it.

pages.title: Security
pages.intent: Security answers 3 questions for every operation: who acts, what it touches, and what it keeps. This page states how a LiteSpec product answers them through authentication, actor resolution, authorization, trust boundaries, secrets, browser defenses, personal data, abuse limits, audit events, and release security checks, for anyone who builds or reviews an operation, an endpoint, a frontend, or a release. A product that follows it proves every operation runs for the right actor, touches only what it may, and keeps sensitive data safe.

pages.title: Testing
pages.intent: Every stack proves its records through the same cross-stack Proof rules: each scenario is proved through the public boundary, each rule through its scenarios, and expected values come from the scenario's Then. This page states those rules, the test projects each size requires, the one mock rule and the mutation gate, while each stack's testing page states how its stack runs them. A project that claims the `proof` layer applies this page, and a team that claims it as its own keeps its own test practice.

pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: The Reference pages list exact values a reader looks up: terms, provision identifiers (IDs citing one rule each), file shapes, schemas, URLs, and the records behind decisions and audit duties. Every project uses them during any task that names a term, cites a provision, or edits a project file. A developer or agent opens them for lookup in the middle of other work, not for reading in order, and they state no rules of their own: each rule lives on the standards page they point to, so these pages stay exact while the rules stay in one place.

pages.title: Audit Obligations
pages.intent: The audit extension is the LiteSpec bundle a project selects to record who attempted what against which target and what it produced; it satisfies obligations from 4 guidance bodies (NIST, ISO, PCI DSS, and OWASP) and from the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). This page states those obligations in one place: the frameworks, the GDPR articles, and the map from each obligation to the provision (one identified rule) that satisfies it. A team writing its audit adoption decision reads it to state that reasoning without surveying the frameworks from scratch; the [Audit Trail](../ext/audit.md) owns every provision, and this page explains and states no rules.

pages.title: Decision Records
pages.intent: A decision record pins one expensive-to-reverse choice (a data model, a provider, a security boundary) down with the options weighed and the evidence cited, so a later team sees why the product looks the way it does instead of relitigating it. This page states where each record lives in the consumer repository (the application repository built against one pinned LiteSpec release), what fields and explanation sections it holds, and how a record changes: in place, with git keeping the history.

pages.title: Finding Codes
pages.intent: Use this generated page to read what a finding code means and how to resolve it. A reader who sees a code in `litespec model check` output, or in a `Checked by` line of a standards page, looks it up here. The table holds every code the tools emit, with its level, the record layer it governs, whether it ties that layer to the records, and the extension that adds it.

pages.title: Record Folders
pages.intent: Use this generated page to find the folder and file each record type lives in, relative to `.litespec/`. A record in any other folder is a `record-placement-invalid` finding. The Flat module column marks a home that applies only to a module that keeps its records flat.

pages.title: Formats
pages.intent: Every file a LiteSpec tool reads or writes has one format, and every format a person writes has one schema (a contract stating its exact shape) that the checking command and the editor both validate. This page lists each format: the file, who writes it, its envelope, the command that reads or checks it, and its schema with a real example. An author in a consumer project uses it to wire editor validation and to look up a field, and a tool author uses it to find which command owns which file.

pages.title: Release Manifest
pages.intent: `litespec.manifest.yaml` is the inventory of one LiteSpec release (one published version of the standard): the technology stacks, project shapes, extensions, and pinned versions it ships. A LiteSpec maintainer edits it when the release gains a stack or an extension, while a consumer (an application repository built against one pinned release) never edits it and instead pins the whole release and records the version it reviewed. This page lists every field with the current release's real values and states what each field drives.

pages.title: Project File
pages.intent: `.litespec/project.yaml` is the one record of what a consumer project (an application repository built against one pinned LiteSpec release) selected: its size, shape, technology stacks, extensions, paths, and pinned release. The team edits it when the selection changes and validates it with the `litespec model check` command before relying on it. This page lists every field the file holds, states what reads each field, and shows the errors a wrong value produces.

pages.title: Provisions
pages.intent: Use this generated page to resolve a provision ID to its heading, owning page, scope, record layer, trace, strength, and verification mark, and to read the checked share of rules for each page.

pages.title: Published URLs
pages.intent: An agent (software that reads task context, changes files, and runs checks) wires itself to LiteSpec through URLs on `https://litespec.dev`, not through a local copy of the repository. This page lists every URL the site serves: its pattern, a real example for the current release, and what it returns, so an agent or a reader resolves any reference with a fetch.

pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: The Tools section documents the LiteSpec command line: one command for each consumer check, generator, and lookup, from project validation to generated files. A developer or coding assistant opens this index to find the command that produces the check or file the task needs. On a command page, Name and Synopsis give the quick form, and Description and Examples give the detail. The commands that maintain the standard itself live in the [Maintain overview](../maintain/README.md).

pages.title: Book Command
pages.intent: `litespec book` - Generate the project book, one offline shell with sharded data, from a consumer root.

pages.title: Initialize Consumer
pages.intent: `litespec init` starts a consumer repository from a preset, a ready-made selection of shape, stacks, frontends, and layer claims, or the records preset, which claims the record model with no stacks.

pages.title: Model Builder
pages.intent: `litespec model` checks the project model, formats record files, renders generated outputs, and answers record queries.

pages.title: Scaffold Record
pages.intent: `litespec new` scaffolds a record file and reserves its identifier, appends a result or scenario entry to a use-case file, or appends a requirement, rule, permission, or setting entry to its owning list file.

pages.title: Rename Record
pages.intent: `litespec rename` renames a record identifier and rewrites every link.

pages.title: Rules Query
pages.intent: `litespec rules` lists the provisions that govern a path or a record identifier at the record layers the project claims in [layers](../core/scope.md#layer-claims).

pages.title: Start a Consumer Repository
pages.intent: A LiteSpec consumer is a project built against the LiteSpec standard, and this tutorial turns an empty folder into one: its configuration, its first Intent records, the Behavior specified from them, one working use case, and a passing model check. A use case names what the product does for an actor, a person or system using it, and the model check confirms the records, code, and tests agree. This tutorial follows one backend stack and one frontend stack, the `dotnet` backend with a React frontend, so every step runs the same way for every reader. A developer follows these steps once, when creating the consumer. Each step names the standard it satisfies, and the tutorial adds no rule of its own.

pages.title: Model a Behavior Module
pages.intent: A behavior module gathers one business area's glossary terms, aggregates, rules, use cases, reactions, jobs, notifications, settings, events, and permissions into record files that the model builder, the tool that checks the project, reads. This tutorial works through one kind of record at a time, using the spending module of the Claimwick product as the worked example. Each step names the standard it satisfies, and the tutorial adds no rule of its own.

pages.title: Overview
pages.intent: The Workspace pages state the shape every repository built with LiteSpec shares: the canonical monorepo tree, the names that expose architectural role, the packages each layer, from Domain to the API host, may take, and where each configuration value lives. Every project applies them, whatever its size, shape, or technology stacks.

pages.title: Configuration
pages.intent: Configuration is every value a workspace sets outside code: version pins, backend and frontend settings, environment access, secrets, and toolchain versions. This page states where each value lives, who owns it, and when a bad value fails. It applies to anyone who adds a setting, a dependency, or a tool to the workspace.

pages.title: Dependencies
pages.intent: Dependencies are the packages a codebase takes on, and each one adds updates, advisories, and migration work. This page states which dependencies each layer, from Domain to the API host, may take, where each package version is pinned, and what a new package needs before it lands. It applies to anyone who adds a package, references another layer, or connects two frontends.

pages.title: Naming and Code Style
pages.intent: Names are the first documentation a reader meets: a name states the business intent and architectural role without opening the file. In a LiteSpec codebase every architectural role carries a fixed suffix, every type an aggregate owns starts with its root's name, and every frontend file follows one casing map. This page states those suffixes, anchors, and casings, with the exception-naming, boolean, async, and language-version rules beside them, for anyone who names code, and especially for agents working across sessions.

pages.title: Workspace Structure
pages.intent: A LiteSpec consumer, a project built with LiteSpec, keeps one monorepo tree for its applications, shared packages, documentation, tests, and records. This page states that tree, where each file kind lives inside it, and what `.litespec/project.yaml` declares. It applies to anyone who creates a file, and to agents locating code without asking.
